name: Micro employer — first repeatable payroll
size:
Payroll software for micro businesses / startups
Illustrative: 1–20 employees; usually one employing entity.
readiness: Salary agreements, bank details and leave records may be incomplete or arrive by message. First use case: create a checked employee master before calculating pay.
complexity: Mostly fixed monthly salaries, occasional joiners/leavers and reimbursements. A shift-heavy small employer can need a different process despite the same size.
people: Founder or office administrator; often no dedicated HR/payroll role. Need guided setup and a repeatable monthly checklist.
Founder/accountant reviews totals and authorises payment; the accountant may advise without owning the software.
A team lead supplies approved changes where needed; a formal multi-level hierarchy is not assumed.
industries: Startup payroll: salary changes and joiner proration → reviewed monthly pay → payslips.
Small retail payroll: agreed attendance and paid days → salary calculation → proprietor approval.
Small agency payroll: employee salaries and approved reimbursements → payroll. Keep contractor invoices separate.
departments: Collect employee changes and leave; maintain one current employee list.
Review pay totals, authorise bank payment and record the payroll expense.
technology: Spreadsheet or basic employee list: require a checked initial import, not a full HRIS integration by default.
Leave register or simple attendance export: reconcile only the inputs that affect pay.
Accountant's ledger and bank portal: require consistent journals and payment files; no native connector assumed.
Excel/paper to payroll: validate employee details, opening balances and a sample pay run before migration.
trigger: First recurring employees, founder spending too long on payroll, or an accountant requesting consistent monthly inputs.

name: Growing small business — HR-led payroll
size:
Payroll software for small businesses
Illustrative: 21–75 employees; one entity with a growing team.
readiness: HR maintains records but managers send attendance, reimbursements and changes separately. Use case: agree owners and cut-off dates before importing.
complexity: Joiners/leavers, leave adjustments and occasional variable pay; headcount alone does not establish complicated payroll.
people: An HR generalist or administrator owns preparation; one payroll-responsible person may share other HR duties.
Owner or finance lead checks the register and funding before release; external adviser may review exceptions.
Department heads approve their team's attendance and one-off pay inputs, not separate payroll engines.
industries: SaaS/IT payroll: maintain salary revisions, joiner/leaver dates and approved incentives → calculate monthly payroll.
Small workshop payroll: approved shifts and overtime → reviewed payable earnings. Only relevant where time-based pay exists.
Retail payroll: store attendance and approved incentive totals → consolidate → pay.
Small clinic payroll: approved employee rosters and allowances → payroll; visiting consultants may be outside employee payroll.
Agency payroll: employee pay and approved bonus/reimbursement inputs → calculate and review.
departments: HR changes and leave → payroll preparation → employee payslip access.
Payroll register → owner/finance approval → bank file and accounting entry.
Where commissions exist: sales manager approves the incentive total → payroll imports it; payroll need not calculate sales performance.
technology: Basic HRMS employee master: check employee IDs, dates and pay fields at import.
Separate attendance/leave application: require approved period totals and traceable corrections.
Accounting package and bank portal: export approved liabilities, journals and payment instructions.
Spreadsheet interfaces: standardise templates and reconcile employee and pay totals during rollout.
trigger: Hiring the first HR generalist, repeated input chasing at month-end, or moving away from an accountant-managed spreadsheet.

name: Established SMB — coordinated HR and payroll
size:
Payroll software for SMBs
Illustrative: 76–200 employees; departmental handoffs are becoming material.
readiness: Employee, attendance and expense data come from several owners. Reconcile missing records, duplicates and late approvals before payroll.
complexity: Several pay components and departments; one or a few sites. Workforce mix and pay policies matter more than the size label.
people: Illustrative small HR team with an HR manager and payroll/operations owner; a dedicated specialist is optional.
Finance reviewer owns funding and posting; separate preparation from final authorisation where required.
Managers approve time, leave and variable-pay inputs; HR resolves missing or conflicting approvals.
industries: IT/services payroll: revised salaries, leave, reimbursements and approved incentives → validated gross-to-net run.
Manufacturing payroll: shift attendance, approved overtime and absences → time-linked earnings → review.
Retail/e-commerce payroll: store or warehouse attendance and approved incentives → location-wise validation → payroll.
Healthcare payroll: employee rosters and approved shift/on-call allowances → checked pay components.
Professional-services payroll: approved employee pay changes and cost-centre assignments → payroll and costing outputs; not client billing.
departments: HR/payroll collects lifecycle and absence changes, resolves exceptions and publishes payslips.
Finance reviews variances, approves payment and reconciles accounting outputs.
Sales operations supplies approved commissions; payroll checks the approved amount and period before payment.
technology: HRIS data: map salary-effective dates and lifecycle changes into payroll.
Attendance/leave exports or interfaces: reconcile employee IDs, period boundaries and loss-of-pay inputs.
Accounting/ERP interface: map cost centres and ledger codes; confirm actual import/export support.
Legacy payroll migration: reconcile year-to-date values, salary structures and a parallel sample run; avoid assuming a native migration tool.
trigger: More payroll corrections, fragmented attendance/HR tools, an HR team reorganisation, or a decision to bring payroll operations in-house.

name: Mid-market employer — controlled payroll close
size:
Payroll software for mid-market companies
Illustrative: 201–500 employees; size can overlap with other operating contexts.
readiness: Multiple administrators submit changes and adjustments. Use case: validated cut-off snapshots, named exception owners and reviewable changes.
complexity: Multiple salary structures, sites or pay groups; monthly payroll may include arrears and final settlements. Multiple entities are possible, not required.
people: Payroll specialist plus HR operations contributors; HR manager owns policy and exceptions. Actual staffing depends on automation and scope.
Finance controller/approver checks variances, funding and posting; responsibilities should be separated from preparation.
Managers own source approvals; local HR reviews site inputs before central payroll accepts them.
industries: SaaS/IT payroll: salary revisions and approved variable pay → variance review → controlled release.
Manufacturing payroll: time-pay adjustments and approved allowances → exception review before release.
Retail/e-commerce payroll: consolidate location inputs and employee transfers → reconcile → release.
Healthcare payroll: approved roster and allowance changes → exception handling → payroll close.
Professional-services payroll: pay changes, bonuses and cost allocations → review and reconcile, separate from billing or revenue recognition.
departments: HR operations and payroll: source changes → exceptions → reviewed run → employee queries.
Finance: variance review → approval → payment and journal reconciliation.
Sales/compensation owners: approve incentive inputs and corrections → hand off to payroll with traceability.
technology: Core HR integration requirement: controlled effective-dated employee and salary changes.
Attendance/leave interface requirement: approved snapshots, failed-import visibility and adjustment traceability.
ERP/accounting requirement: cost-centre mapping and reconciliation of journals against the approved register.
Payroll replacement: parallel calculations and opening-balance checks; validate exports/APIs before promising connectors.
trigger: Payroll close relies on too many spreadsheets or private messages, recurring audit/reconciliation effort, or replacing a fragmented HR/payroll setup.

name: Attendance-heavy multi-site employer
size:
Payroll software for multi-site and frontline workforces
Illustrative: 201–1,500 employees; can also fit smaller shift-heavy employers.
readiness: Site devices, rosters and local approvers create late or inconsistent time inputs. Use case: reconcile approved attendance before it changes pay.
complexity: Sites, shifts, overtime rules and frequent workforce changes drive complexity. Separate employees from contractor/vendor billing; labels alone do not determine legal status.
people: Central payroll owner and local HR/time administrators; staffing follows sites and input workload rather than a fixed employee ratio.
Central finance reviews site totals, pay variances and bank release.
Site supervisors approve time and overtime; central payroll resolves unmatched IDs, missing approvals and corrections.
industries: IT/BPO operations with shifts: approved shift/attendance changes → payroll adjustments; not every software company needs this.
Manufacturing/mining payroll: site attendance and approved time/allowances → local validation → central payroll. Validate site policies separately.
Retail/e-commerce payroll: store, warehouse and field attendance → transfers and variable inputs → consolidated payroll.
Hospital payroll: employee rosters and approved duty allowances → checked time-linked earnings.
Field-service payroll: approved employee time/allowances by site → pay and cost allocation; supplier charges remain separate.
departments: HR/site operations → reviewed attendance and employee changes → payroll exceptions.
Finance → reconcile site/pay-group totals → approve release → cost-centre posting.
Sales/store managers → approved incentive totals → payroll; not an assumed sales-commission calculation module.
technology: Employee master must consistently identify location, employing entity and effective transfers.
Time/roster or biometric-system feeds: require mapping, cut-offs and correction handling; device/vendor support must be verified.
Accounting output needs site/cost-centre mappings and reconciliation to payroll totals.
Mixed site spreadsheets/legacy tools: staged migration with site-by-site input validation and parallel pay checks.
trigger: New sites or shift patterns, recurring attendance-related pay disputes, late site submissions, or a need to centralise payroll without losing local approvals.

name: Enterprise — specialist teams and shared services
size:
Payroll software for enterprises
Illustrative: 1,000–5,000 employees; overlaps are intentional, not a strict maturity boundary.
readiness: Several source systems and approval owners require controlled interfaces, complete period inputs and audit-ready change history.
complexity: Pay groups, business units, locations and exceptions create reconciliation work. Scale alone does not prove every employee has complex pay.
people: Payroll manager and payroll specialists with HR shared-services contributors; staffing and segregation follow workload and risk.
Controller/treasury and accounting reviewers separate funding, authorisation and reconciliation responsibilities.
Business-unit/site approvers provide certified inputs; shared services handles employee payroll questions.
industries: IT/services enterprise payroll: governed salary/variable-pay changes across business units → reviewed payroll close.
Manufacturing/mining enterprise payroll: site-specific time/pay inputs → policy validation → central oversight.
Retail/e-commerce enterprise payroll: workforce movements and location inputs → exception ownership → coordinated release.
Healthcare group payroll: approved employee rosters/allowances across facilities → shared payroll controls.
Professional-services enterprise payroll: employee compensation and cost allocations → entity/unit review → reporting; client project revenue is separate.
departments: Shared HR/payroll operations: standard intake → owned exceptions → maker/checker review → employee service.
Finance/treasury: pay-group and unit reconciliation → funding/approval → payment/ledger close.
Compensation/sales operations: certify variable-pay inputs and adjustments → payroll with an approval trail.
technology: Enterprise HRIS requirement: authoritative master data, effective dating and access-controlled changes.
Workforce-management feeds: approved snapshots and visibility into failed or late inputs.
ERP requirement: controlled journal formats, cost allocation and reconciliation; named ERP compatibility requires verification.
Legacy replacement: phased parallel runs, historical balance reconciliation, permissions and support handover.
trigger: Shared-services rollout, system replacement, growing close-control requirements, or too much reconciliation across payroll and finance.

name: Corporate group — multi-entity payroll governance
size:
Payroll software for large groups and multi-entity employers
Illustrative: 5,000+ employees; multi-entity needs may arise much earlier.
readiness: Different entities/source owners require consistent identifiers and reconciliation without erasing local rules or data ownership.
complexity: Entity, location and pay-group differences matter. India is the current market; international entities require separately verified country coverage, not an assumed global payroll feature.
people: Group payroll lead and entity payroll teams/shared services; local subject-matter reviewers where needed.
Entity finance plus group treasury/consolidation; approve entity runs before group-level reporting.
Entity/site approvers own local inputs; group governance defines controls and escalation.
industries: IT group payroll: approved compensation changes by employing entity → entity runs → group cost reporting.
Industrial group payroll: plant/mining-site inputs and local approved policies → entity payroll → central oversight.
Retail/e-commerce group payroll: legal-entity and location mappings → approved pay runs → consolidated reporting.
Healthcare group payroll: facility inputs and entity ownership → governed payroll release and consolidation.
Professional-services group payroll: compensation and allocation changes by entity → local review → group reporting.
departments: Group HR/payroll: common intake controls with entity-specific rules and exception ownership.
Entity finance/group treasury: approved payroll results → funding and reconciliation → consolidated cost view.
Compensation/sales teams: approved incentive allocations across employing entities → relevant payroll run.
technology: One or several HRIS sources: identify the source of truth per entity and govern employee transfers.
Multiple workforce systems: standardise interface contracts while keeping relevant local pay inputs.
Multiple accounting/ERP ledgers: entity-level journals and cross-system reconciliation; no claim of universal ERP compatibility.
Acquisition/legacy consolidation: staged cutovers, retained history and reconciled balances; country packs are a separate validation gate.
trigger: Acquisitions, group-wide payroll consolidation, divergent entity processes, or a need for central visibility with local accountability.
